### Feature Description

falcon-mcp has no documentation-retrieval tool. An agent connected to the server can query the tenant in depth (29 modules today) but cannot look up CrowdStrike's own documentation — it has to fall back on whatever the model memorized, which for a platform that ships API changes continuously is the weakest link in the chain.

I'd like a `docs` module. Concretely, two capabilities, in priority order:

**1. API reference lookup (no credentials required).**
`developer.crowdstrike.com` already publishes an LLM-addressable mirror of the entire API reference:

- `https://developer.crowdstrike.com/llms.txt`
- `https://developer.crowdstrike.com/llms-full.txt` — 1468 operations, each with method, path and required scope (~380 KB)
- a `.md` variant of every reference page, e.g. `https://developer.crowdstrike.com/api-reference/operations/QueryDevicesByFilter.md`, which returns method, path, `**Scope:** Hosts: READ`, the parameter list, and a FalconPy example in under 1 KB
- `https://developer.crowdstrike.com/api-reference/operations-by-collection.md`

All of the above are public, unauthenticated, `200`, and already clean Markdown. Two tools over that surface — search the operation catalogue, fetch one operation page — need no new credentials and no new scopes.

**2. Product documentation search (credentialed).**
The product documentation is a different story, and this is the part I can't solve on my own:

- `https://falcon.<region>.crowdstrike.com/documentation/page/<id>/<slug>` returns the Falcon **login page** to any non-browser client — it's an Ember SPA behind a console session cookie.
- `https://docs.crowdstrike.com` is a Fluid Topics instance (`<meta name="ft-tenant-base-url" content="https://docs.crowdstrike.com/">`). Its REST API is live but gated: `GET /api/users/me` → `401 {"error":"Unauthorized","message":"Required Authentication"}`. Fluid Topics documents search/maps/topics endpoints and JWT + SSO auth, so there is a real machine-readable docs API here — just not one a Falcon API client can reach.
- The Falcon API itself has no documentation collection. I went through all 128 collections / 1468 operations in `llms-full.txt`: the only near-miss is `Knowledge Bases` / `Knowledge Base Files` (`/agentic-studio/...`, scope *Charlotte AI Agent Definition*), which is the customer-authored corpus for Charlotte AI agents, not CrowdStrike product docs. FalconPy's 135 endpoint modules confirm the same.
- The regional Swagger spec is not public either — `https://assets.falcon.crowdstrike.com/support/api/swagger.json` returns `403 MissingKey` ("Missing Key-Pair-Id query parameter or cookie value"), i.e. a signed CloudFront URL minted by a console session.

So: **an OAuth2 API client pair — the only credential falcon-mcp holds — cannot retrieve CrowdStrike product documentation today.** If that's something CrowdStrike would consider exposing (a docs search operation under an existing or new scope, or a documented way to use a Fluid Topics token alongside the Falcon creds), it would make part 2 buildable. If not, I'd rather know that than keep guessing, and part 1 still stands on its own.

### Use Case

As a security engineer driving falcon-mcp from an agent, the failures I hit are documentation failures, not API failures:

- **Scope errors.** An agent picks a tool, the call 403s, and the fix is knowing the exact scope string. Today that lives in a hand-maintained mapping inside this repo — which is precisely what #545, #552 and #553 were about. A live lookup against `developer.crowdstrike.com`, where the scope is stated on every operation page, turns that from data this project has to keep correct into data it can read.
- **Reaching past the MCP.** When no tool covers what I need, the next step is a direct FalconPy/REST call. Right now the agent guesses the operation ID, path and parameters from memory. With an API-reference tool it can look up `operations-by-collection.md`, confirm the operation exists, and get the signature — in the same session, without me leaving to open a browser.
- **Product behaviour, not just endpoints.** Half my questions aren't "what's the endpoint" but "what does this prevention-policy setting actually do", "what does this sensor status mean", "what are the documented limits on RTR". Those answers are only in the product docs. That is the auth-walled half above, and it's the half I'd get the most out of.

The distinctive thing here is that the credential is already in the room. I'm authenticated to the tenant; the docs I need are gated by the same subscription I'm authenticated against. Making the server able to read them is a much shorter path than any external docs mirror.

### Related Module/Area

New module needed

### Proposed Solution (Optional)

A `docs` module, with part 1 shippable independently of part 2:

```
falcon_search_api_reference(query, collection=None, limit=20)
    -> [{operation_id, method, path, scope, summary, doc_url}]
    Backed by developer.crowdstrike.com/llms-full.txt (or operations-by-collection.md),
    fetched once and cached. No auth.

falcon_get_api_operation(operation_id)
    -> full operation page (params, scope, example)
    Backed by /api-reference/operations/<OperationId>.md. No auth.

falcon_search_product_docs(query, limit=10)      # part 2, gated
falcon_get_product_doc(doc_id)                   # part 2, gated
    Backed by the docs.crowdstrike.com Fluid Topics API, registered only when a
    docs credential is configured, and absent from tools/list otherwise.
```

Notes on fit with existing conventions:

- Part 1 introduces the server's first outbound call to a host other than the Falcon API. That's a real design decision, not a detail — it wants an opt-out (the module is already opt-in via `--modules`), and it needs to honour the existing proxy configuration from #405.
- Alternatively part 1 could ship as MCP **resources** rather than tools, alongside the existing `falcon_mcp/resources/*.py` FQL guides. Resources are the closer analogue — they're reference material, not actions. Tools are the better fit only because the operation catalogue is too large to hand to a client wholesale; it needs a query. Happy to go either way.
- Part 2 must degrade silently. A tool that's registered but always 401s is worse than one that isn't there.

### Alternatives Considered (Optional)

- **Point a generic web-fetch tool at the docs.** Works for part 1 and is what I do now, but it means the agent has to already know the URL scheme, and it does nothing for part 2 — an unauthenticated fetch of a `/documentation/page/...` URL returns the login page, which the model then cheerfully summarizes as though it were documentation. That failure is silent, which is what makes it worth fixing inside this server.
- **Widen the embedded `resources/*.py` guides into a full docs corpus.** Doesn't scale, and it recreates the staleness problem this request is trying to remove.
- **A separate CrowdStrike docs MCP server.** Cleaner separation, but it splits the credential story across two servers for what is, from the agent's point of view, one platform. I'd rather it lived here — though if CrowdStrike would rather ship it standalone, that answers the question just as well.
- **Scrape the console with a session cookie.** Explicitly not proposing this. It's fragile, it's not a supported interface, and it isn't something this server should be doing.

### Additional Context (Optional)

Everything above was verified against the live endpoints on 2026-08-31, from a US-2 tenant.

Related open issues: #522 (CAO hunting saved queries and guides) touches adjacent ground — surfacing CrowdStrike-authored hunting content — but through the tenant API rather than the documentation. #440 (making `resources/*.py` the single source of truth for FQL hints) overlaps with the "resources vs tools" question in part 1.

Happy to open a PR for part 1 if the approach and the outbound-host question look acceptable. Part 2 I can't build without a supported way in, which is really what I'm asking about.

## Why

Nearly every Android bug in this player's history lived in the hand-written producer layer (extractor + `AMediaCodec` state machine + AAudio): the non-monotonic pacing traps, AAudio power-saving underruns, the audio wedge, and most recently the read-error-is-EOS bug fixed in #70 (v1.9.6). Each one cost a device session to find. AndroidX Media3 (ExoPlayer) has already paid for all of them: `Mp4Extractor`, `DefaultAudioSink` with a latency-corrected position tracker, load-error retry policy, seek/loop state machine, and a decade of per-device codec quirks.

What is genuinely ours and must stay identical: the OpenXR frame loop, the Vulkan `AHardwareBuffer` import and weaving hand-off, display-locked frame selection against the runtime's predicted display time, exact-PTS L/R pairing for dual-track stereo MP4 (LVF v2), the convergence UV shift, and the shared ImGui HUD. None of that touches the producer.

This issue scopes replacing the **producer** (extractor + codec + audio output) with ExoPlayer driven from Kotlin over JNI, while the **consumer** (`AImageReader` onward) stays native. Two research passes went into it: an audit of the current contract in `video_decoder.cpp` / `audio_player.cpp` / `main.cpp`, and a primary-source read of androidx/media `1.10.0`. Findings below cite both.

**Not a rewrite now.** v1.9.6 is robust and device-verified. This is the plan for the next real expansion of the Android player (streaming, subtitles, HDR, DRM, 4K60-per-eye tuning), or when the producer bites again.

## Verdict

Feasible, as **"ExoPlayer + four small custom classes"**. We would not adopt ExoPlayer's rendering model; we use its extractor / codec / audio plumbing and override its frame-release policy so the native consumer keeps owning presentation. Estimated 450–650 LOC Kotlin + ~150 LOC JNI + a ~200 LOC consumer refactor; deletes ~1,400 LOC of native producer code.

| # | Finding (androidx/media 1.10.0) | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `MediaCodecVideoRenderer.renderOutputBufferV21` calls `codec.releaseOutputBuffer(index, releaseTimeNs)` with a **vsync-snapped `System.nanoTime()`** (`VideoFrameReleaseHelper.adjustReleaseTime`, 80 % vsync offset). Our consumer reads `AImage_getTimestamp()` as the **media PTS** (today the codec is released with `presentationTimeUs*1000`). As-is this breaks display-locked selection *and* L/R pairing, and trips `validatePtsOnce` into the newest-frame fallback. | **Feasible with a subclass**: override `renderOutputBufferV21` (protected) to release at `presentationTimeUs * 1000`. An `AImageReader` consumer never applies desired-present-time deferral, so the value is pure metadata, exactly as today. Zero consumer change. (`VideoFrameMetadataListener` is the weaker alternative: exact, but per-frame on the playback thread and unavailable on the effects path.) |
| 2 | **Two video renderers on one player**: no stock support. `DefaultTrackSelector.selectAllTracks` yields one definition per track type; `MappingTrackSelector.selectTracks` is `final` and `preferUnassociatedRenderer` is hard-coded to metadata only. | **Feasible with a custom class**: implement `TrackSelector` directly (maintainer-endorsed pattern, google/ExoPlayer#6589, re-confirmed androidx/media#1473) returning two `FixedTrackSelection`s at the two video renderer indices. Engine has no per-type limit; the only constraint (one `MediaClock`) is satisfied because video renderers return `null` from `getMediaClock()`. Surfaces per renderer via `createMessage(renderer).setType(MSG_SET_VIDEO_OUTPUT)`, never `setVideoSurface` (broadcasts). |
| 3 | The two video renderers are **not synchronised to each other**: each owns a `VideoFrameReleaseControl` and independently drops (`earlyUs < -30 ms`), drops-to-keyframe (`< -500 ms`) and force-releases. | **Real hazard, neutralisable**: override `shouldDropOutputBuffer` / `shouldDropBuffersToKeyframe` → `false` in both renderers and let the native pairing queue absorb jitter. ExoPlayer becomes a decode pump driven by one audio clock. |
| 4 | `tkhd` disabled flag is **never read** by `BoxParser.parseTkhd`; both eye tracks appear as `C.TRACK_TYPE_VIDEO`. `hdlr` name is not read; `mdhd` language → `Format.language`, `tkhd` track id → `Format.id`. | **Go.** Discriminate L/R by `Format.language` (`abl`/`abr`), fall back to track order, same rule as the native probe. |
| 5 | The `mett` convergence track is exposed (`parseMetaDataSampleEntry` keeps the MIME verbatim) but needs `MimeTypes.registerCustomMimeType(..., TRACK_TYPE_METADATA)` plus a custom `MetadataDecoderFactory` to be decoded; and `elst` is applied **per track**, so a convergence track without its own edit list is not shifted with the video. | **Keep it native.** The existing probe already parses it once at open into an array indexed by PTS. Routing it through a Java looper callback is strictly more machinery and reintroduces the edit-list trap. |
| 6 | Audio position: `getCurrentPosition()` is ms-granular, app-thread-only, refreshed every ~10 ms. The accurate value (`MediaCodecAudioRenderer.getPositionUs` → `AudioTrackPositionTracker`, `AudioTrack.getTimestamp`, latency-corrected) is playback-thread-only. | **Feasible with a subclass**: `MediaCodecAudioRenderer` override of `getPositionUs()` publishes a `(positionUs, nanoTime)` anchor into atomics on every `doSomeWork`; native extrapolates lock-free. Seek: `SeekParameters.EXACT` default; a frame is force-released after a seek while paused. | **Go.** |

## The one change ExoPlayer forces on the consumer

The current slave decoder honours an **occupancy gate**: it releases a frame only when the reader holds nothing unacquired, because an `AImageReader` BufferQueue with an app-controlled producer *and* consumer **replaces** a queued-but-unacquired buffer instead of blocking (`video_decoder.h` "BufferQueue-replace trap"; the "first cycle flat, fine after the loop" report). ExoPlayer cannot honour that gate. So the consumer must stop acquiring on the render tick and instead **drain from an `AImageReader_ImageListener`** (native looper thread) into an app-owned ring of `AImage`s the render thread selects from. The listener fires per queued buffer, so the replace window shrinks to the callback latency instead of a whole render tick, and it also removes the per-tick catch-up polling. Frame selection (`acquireFrameForDisplayTime`, `acquireFrameByPts`, 1 µs pairing slack, stale/stall rules) then operates on the ring unchanged.

## Contract the backend must satisfy (from the audit)

- `AImage_getTimestamp()` = media PTS in ns (finding 1).
- Display-locked selection stays in the consumer (the judder fix is the *consumer* choosing the frame by predicted display time; producer-side pacing lands either side of a vsync).
- Exact-PTS L/R pairing with 1 µs slack; both eyes pause/seek/loop together; slave never paces or drops.
- A master clock that is monotone while playing, and the existing stale-clock guard (frozen ≥500 ms → free-run) kept as belt and braces.
- Teardown that never blocks on a full reader (today's drain-while-joining exists because the codec looper parks on `releaseOutputBufferAtTime`; ExoPlayer's `release()` on the playback thread must be checked for the same shape with the ring still holding images).
- Three independent readers of one SAF fd today (left, right, probe) become: URI string → Java for playback, one dup'd fd → native probe for convergence + eye-track identification.
- `debug.dxr.mp.*` props and the `CADENCE` / `[LVF]` / `#54 DIAG` / `AUDIO` lines survive; they are how every bug above was found. `AUDIO DIAG` is replaced by the Media3 analytics listener equivalents.
- `_noreconv` name rule, `apply_layout` outcomes (`NotLvf` / `Dual` / `FlatLeft`), `resetVideoAhb()` per clip switch: unchanged.

## Design

**Kotlin `Media3Backend`** (one file, built on a dedicated `HandlerThread` looper so `verifyApplicationThread` is satisfied off the UI thread):
- `PtsStampingVideoRenderer : MediaCodecVideoRenderer` — release at PTS, never drop.
- `ClockPublishingAudioRenderer : MediaCodecAudioRenderer` — publish `(positionUs, nanoTime)` anchor.
- `StereoRenderersFactory : RenderersFactory` — `[videoL, videoR, audio]`, no text/metadata/image renderers.
- `StereoTrackSelector : TrackSelector` — the #6589 pattern; assigns eye tracks by `Format.language` then order; mono files enable only `videoL`.
- Glue: `open(uri | fd)`, `setSurfaces(l, r)`, `play/pause/seek(us)`, `setRepeat`, `release`; `Player.Listener` → `onPrepared(durationUs, w, h, fps)`, `onEnded`, `onError`. Native reads the clock anchor through a direct `ByteBuffer`, not a JNI call per frame.

**Native**: `VideoDecoder` keeps its `AImageReader`, hands `ANativeWindow_toSurface()` upward, gains the image-listener ring, keeps `acquireFrameForDisplayTime` / `acquireFrameByPts` / `validatePtsOnce` / stall watchdog verbatim; loses `openFd/start/decodeLoop/rebuildExtractor/slewToAudio` and the codec/extractor teardown. `AudioPlayer` is deleted; its `clockThunk` becomes the anchor extrapolation. `lvf_probe_android` unchanged (keeps `mediandk` linked). `main.cpp` open flow passes the URI up instead of `detachFd()` for playback.

**Gradle**: `androidx.media3:media3-exoplayer:1.10.0` pinned exactly (`minSdk 23`; ours is 29). APK +1–2 MB with R8 (unmeasured).

## Phases (each independently verifiable on the tablet)

1. **Spike, no consumer change** (the go/no-go): Media3 dep + the four classes; open a *mono* SBS clip via ExoPlayer into the existing `AImageReader`; assert on-device that `AImage_getTimestamp()` == media PTS (`validatePtsOnce` stays selectable) and `CADENCE` shows flat-2 at 24 fps. Fails → stop here, the plan is void.
2. **Dual-track**: `StereoTrackSelector` + second surface; assert `[LVF] final pairing` matched == presented across 20 seeks and 5 loops, `miss` in the tens, no L/R straddle beyond the loop seam.
3. **Consumer ring**: image-listener drain replacing tick acquisition + occupancy gate; re-run phases 1–2 plus the 3840×1080 clip that exposed the BufferQueue replace trap.
4. **Audio clock**: anchor atomics replace `AudioPlayer`; A/V offset measured against v1.9.6 on the same clip (the current clock is "PTS just written", leading audible by the buffer depth; the new one is the true playhead, so the anchored offset moves and must be re-measured, not assumed).
5. **Delete** the native producer, teardown-hang test (open a second clip 20× in one process), read-error injection (`debug.dxr.mp.*` fault prop or a FUSE-slow storage), release-signed build, mini-window and prove-3d harness, then release.

## Risks, ranked

1. Unstable API surface: `MediaCodecVideoRenderer`, `VideoFrameReleaseControl`, `TrackSelector` internals are `@UnstableApi`; the `final selectTracks` + hard-coded `preferUnassociatedRenderer` are exactly what shifts between minors. Pin, and gate upgrades behind the phase-2 pairing test.
2. L/R divergence under load if any drop hook is missed in either renderer: surfaces as one-eye starvation in the pairing counters, not corruption.
3. BufferQueue replace during the phase-1/2 window (before the ring lands): expect `miss` counts; do not read them as a Media3 defect.
4. Teardown parking on a full reader with a library-owned release path.
5. A/V alignment shift from the clock semantics change (phase 4 measures it).
6. Net gain is smaller than it looks: after overriding release timing, drop policy and track selection, what we adopt is `Mp4Extractor` + `DefaultAudioSink` + seek/loop + load-error retry. That is still where the bugs were, but it is the honest size of the win.

## Not doing

- `setVideoEffects` / `VideoFrameProcessor` path (stamps system time, metadata listener gets `TIME_UNSET`).
- Convergence through `MetadataRenderer`.
- Two `ExoPlayer` instances (two clocks = the drift this design exists to prevent).
- Any change to desktop (FFmpeg) or to the OpenXR / Vulkan side.

Refs: #69, #70 (why), the pairing traps in `video_decoder.h`, KBXR §6.5a.

## Work Package Contract — P2-WP012

**Title:** Production Orchestrator & Staged Approval State Machine
**Owner authorization:** APPROVED in chat on 2026-09-06
**Canonical branch:** `main`
**Live starting main HEAD:** `3be8ffed28f8807ae89bab22fb64a8018a8fbdb7`

> Goal: make Orbis workflow orchestration backend-owned, mode-aware, approval-gated, resumable and genuinely usable from the browser. Do not build a cosmetic wizard or frontend-only state machine.

## Product truth to preserve
- Orbis = cloud-first, provider-independent AI Video Production Orchestrator / Production Control Plane.
- Core V1 modes: STORY / SHORT / LOOP / SCENE.
- Story is NOT mandatory for every mode.
- Automation-first + guided flexibility + explicit human authority.
- Full history / auditable changes / no silent history loss.
- Expensive generation remains approval/cost gated.
- Reuse durable queue, retry/resume, locks, usage ledger and BatchRun from closed WPs.
- Vidu remains current registered VideoProvider; no direct provider calls from orchestrator.

## Current problem to solve
Current UI performs several stage transitions itself and generic project PATCH can directly mutate `Project.status`. That makes workflow truth client-driven and allows invalid/out-of-order transitions. WP012 must establish a canonical backend orchestration boundary and make frontend consume it.

## In scope

### 1. Canonical production-stage model
Define one backend-owned stage/state vocabulary and transition graph for the currently implemented V1 production path, mode-aware for STORY / SHORT / LOOP / SCENE.

The model must distinguish at minimum:
- planning/generated state vs approved state
- active generation state
- blocked/recovery state where applicable
- final review/completion states already present

Do not force SHORT/LOOP/SCENE through Story.

### 2. ProductionOrchestrator service
Implement a canonical service that owns:
- current production state evaluation
- allowed transitions
- transition preconditions
- approval transitions
- pause / continue / resume semantics
- next-best-action computation
- orchestration command dispatch to existing services
- truthful blocked reason(s)

No duplicated transition tables/rules across frontend/endpoints/services.

### 3. Backend-owned transition APIs
Add canonical APIs for:
- read orchestration state / current stage / available actions / next recommended action
- execute an orchestration action
- approve/reject/revise stage where applicable
- read transition/audit history

Generic `PATCH /projects/{id}` must no longer be a bypass for controlled production-stage transitions. Non-stage project metadata updates must continue to work.

### 4. Mode-aware flow
Support actual current V1 structures:
- STORY: Story -> Story approval -> Storyboard -> Storyboard approval -> Shot Plan -> Shot Plan approval -> production generation
- SHORT: compact structure/scene path; no mandatory Story
- LOOP: loop spec/shot path; no mandatory Story/Script
- SCENE: scene/shot path; no mandatory Story

Use existing generation/planning services where possible. Do not implement WP013 ImageProvider.

### 5. Automation modes
Add provider-neutral orchestration preference with clear semantics:
- MANUAL: user explicitly triggers every stage/action
- ASSISTED: system recommends next action and may automate non-chargeable safe planning actions only with truthful UI
- AUTO: may continue through eligible non-blocked stages according to policy, but MUST stop at mandatory human approval/cost gates and must never silently trigger chargeable generation where approval is required

Persist automation preference at project level in a backward-compatible way.

### 6. Approval / pause / resume safety
- Approval state must be backend-authoritative.
- Invalid/out-of-order transition -> fail closed with clear reason.
- Repeated approve/continue requests must be idempotent/repeat-safe.
- Resume after interruption must evaluate repository/database truth, not blindly replay prior steps.
- Locked entities, reconciliation-required work, active jobs, budget caps and existing completed work must remain respected.
- Do not overwrite historical approved/generated assets.

### 7. Audit history
Persist lightweight auditable transition history containing at minimum:
- project_id
- from_state
- to_state or attempted action
- action
- actor/source
- result (APPLIED / NO_OP / BLOCKED / FAILED)
- reason/code
- created_at

Avoid destructive history updates.

### 8. Browser UX that is genuinely usable
Replace frontend-owned stage mutation logic with canonical orchestrator API use.

UI must show:
- current stage in plain language
- one clear primary Recommended Next Action
- secondary actions where valid
- why an action is blocked
- review/approve controls when required
- automation mode (Manual / Assisted / Auto) with understandable descriptions
- truthful progress when jobs are queued/running
- safe recovery action for failure/reconciliation states

Do not expose provider/model complexity in the normal path.

### 9. Existing queue integration
Video generation actions must route through existing canonical generation / BatchResume / durable queue services rather than creating another queue or client-side loops.

The orchestrator may initiate existing bounded operations, but WP011 safety/idempotency/cost behavior must not be weakened.

### 10. Practical end-to-end tests
Implement focused backend + frontend/integration tests proving the system is usable, including at minimum:
- STORY happy path to approved shot plan and video dispatch gate
- SHORT flow without Story
- LOOP flow without Story/Script
- SCENE flow without Story
- invalid stage skip rejected
- generic project PATCH cannot bypass controlled stage transition
- repeated approval/action is idempotent / no duplicate work
- AUTO stops at mandatory approval/cost gate
- ASSISTED recommends but does not silently perform chargeable work
- resume after partial state chooses correct next action
- active/reconciliation/locked/budget-blocked conditions produce truthful blocked reasons
- queue dispatch only after allowed stage
- transition history retained
- frontend primary action follows backend next-action truth, not a duplicated client table

## Performance / scalability guardrails
- No per-shot N+1 orchestration evaluation.

pinned third-party sources; no onboarding path invents a provider model,
pretends a capability exists, or downgrades any trust/egress confirmation.

## Problem

Tapping a nav item leaves the app. The site reads as a map plus a separate
document section, not as one product.

Measured: a tap on Politicians, Dewan, Bills, Sentiment or Projection is a full
document load — **118 KB of `app.js` and 51 KB of `styles.css` re-downloaded and
re-parsed**, map data re-fetched, and the map's zoom and seat selection
discarded. Returning to the map does it all again.

## Root cause

Commit `6c33e18` (#148) removed the in-app views, on the reasoning that #143 had
just repointed the nav at real static pages, leaving the in-app pairs
unreachable. It deleted:

- **five containers** from `frontend/public/index.html`:

That reasoning was half right. Static pages *are* the correct entry point for

server-render for entry, hydrate for in-app navigation.

## 7. Trend Signals

**1. Memory is the New Battleground**
Across OpenClaw (trust tagging, compaction), Hermes (configurable backends), Pi (compaction reliability), and DeepSeek (context degradation), **memory management is the #1 pain point**. Users demand: (a) secure memory (poisoning prevention), (b) efficient memory (no token waste), and (c) reliable memory (no data loss). **Action for developers:** Prioritize memory hygiene features; consider external backend support and trust-based source tagging.

**2. Cost Governance is a Trust Issue**
The $204 runaway bill (OpenClaw), 5x under-billing (LiteLLM), and unsustainable subscription costs (Kimi K3) show that **cost accuracy and control are non-negotiable** for power users. **Action:** Implement per-model usage logging, stall detection, and budget caps. Transparent cost attribution is a differentiator.

**3. Credential Security is Table Stakes**
Multiple projects are fixing credential leaks (OpenHands SDK, OpenClaw, Hermes). Users are actively probing for injection vulnerabilities (DeepSeek R1, DeepSeek V3). **Action:** Assume credentials will leak; implement redaction at every layer (logs, terminal output, error messages, URLs).

**4. Plugin Interoperability is the Next Standard**
The **Agent Plugins spec** (agent-plugins.org) is referenced by OpenHands SDK and Pi, backed by Amazon, Cursor, and Microsoft. This is the ecosystem's answer to fragmentation. **Action:** Align plugin formats with this emerging standard to avoid lock-in.

**5. Windows Support is a Growth Opportunity**
Multiple first-time contributors are fixing Windows issues (OpenHands SDK, Pi, Hermes). The "gazzilion developers on windows" (Pi #7547) represents an underserved segment. **Action:** Invest in Windows CI/CD, PATHEXT-aware process spawning, and installer reliability.

**6. Long-Session Reliability Determines Power-User Retention**
Compaction failures, context degradation, and in-flight tool chain drops are driving power users away. **Action:** Implement compaction checks after every agentic turn, preserve in-flight operations during compression, and add observability for silent failures.

**7. Maintainer Responsiveness is a Competitive Advantage**
Pi's 24-hour bug-fix turnaround and OpenHands SDK's rapid security fixes contrast sharply with DeepSeek's zero maintainer engagement. **Action:** Even a brief acknowledgment of community issues (as Qwen Agent needs for #936) significantly improves contributor retention.

## Problem

In this issue, the **parent** is the worktree where `swt create` runs. A **child** is a worktree that `swt create` makes.

A child keeps no record of its parent. In a parent worktree `issue-42` on the branch `issue-42`, `swt create fix-parser` makes these names:

```text
directory  <directory that holds issue-42>/fix-parser-<token>.swt
branch     swt/fix-parser-<token>
```

Neither name contains `issue-42`. Thus nothing can find the children of a branch:

- An orchestrator starts three subagents, then loses its context. It cannot find their worktrees again.
- A person who is about to merge or delete the parent cannot see that unmerged work is in a child.
- `swt` has no command that shows what it made. The person must read `git worktree list` and guess from the names.

**Expected:**

1. The names of a child show which parent it came from.
2. `swt list`, run in a worktree, shows the children of the branch that the worktree has checked out.
3. A hook or a skill can find the same children with plain git, without `swt`.

## Root Cause Analysis

The naming step of `swt create` builds both names from two inputs only: the name that the caller gives, and a uniqueness token (process id and clock, in base 36). It does not read the branch or the name of the parent worktree.

The directory goes beside the parent. That position does not identify the parent, because many parents share one directory. All worktrees under `tools-worktrees/` put their children into that one directory. The main checkout puts its children into `~/code`, next to every other repository.

Nothing needed the relation until now. `swt merge` reads the branch from the HEAD of the child, and merges into the worktree where it runs. Thus no code recorded the parent.

No other tool in this repository, and no skill in the dotfiles, parses the `swt/` branch prefix or the `.swt` suffix. Only the `swt` tests pin the current format.

## Design

### The key is the branch of the parent

The branch of the parent is the thing that `swt merge` merges into. It is also the thing a tool knows when it asks "does this branch have children?".

| Name | Today | Proposed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Branch | `swt/<name>-<token>` | `swt/<parent-branch>/<name>-<token>` |
| Directory | `<name>-<token>.swt` | `<parent-worktree-name>--<name>-<token>.swt` |

- **The branch keeps the parent branch verbatim.** Git accepts a valid branch name in the middle of a ref, slashes included. `git check-ref-format` accepts `refs/heads/swt/feat/foo/fix-parser-abc`. The part `<name>-<token>` never contains `/`, so the parent is exactly the text between `swt/` and the last `/`. This key loses nothing, so a hash gives no benefit and costs readability.
- **The directory keeps the name of the parent worktree** (the last component of its path), and stays beside the parent. `ls` then shows each child next to its parent. A child of the main checkout becomes `tools--fix-parser-<token>.swt`, not a bare `fix-parser-<token>.swt` in `~/code`. The directory name is for people. `swt list` does not parse it.
- **One token, minted once, keys both names**, as #284 requires.
- **A parent on a detached HEAD has no branch.** `swt create` refuses it before it creates anything, and says why. `swt merge` into a detached parent works today only when the parent did not advance. It reads the parent branch as the literal `HEAD`. When the parent advanced, the rebase step runs `git rebase HEAD` in the child. That command does nothing, so the second fast-forward fails too.

### `swt list`

- Run in any worktree, `swt list` shows the children of the branch that is checked out there.
- Its source is `git worktree list --porcelain -z`, the registry of git. It does not scan directories. The NUL-separated form keeps a path with a newline in one entry.
- A child is shown only when its parent is **equal** to the current branch. A prefix is not sufficient: the children of `feat/foo` are not children of `feat`.
- Each child is one line on stdout: the path, a tab, and the branch. The path comes first, so the output can go directly to `swt merge`.
- When git marks a child `prunable` (its directory is gone), the line gets a third field, `prunable`. The user can then prune it.
- When there are no children, stdout is empty, a note goes to stderr, and the exit status is 0. `[ -n "$(swt list)" ]` is then a complete check.
- On a detached HEAD, `swt list` has no branch to ask about. It exits 1 with a message on stderr.

### A check with plain git

A hook or a skill can find the child branches without `swt`:

```sh
git for-each-ref --format='%(refname:short)' "refs/heads/swt/$(git symbolic-ref --short HEAD)/*"
```

Git 2.55 gives these results. In `for-each-ref`, `*` does not cross `/`, so the pattern for `feat` shows only the children of `feat`. Two similar commands are wrong:

- `git branch --list 'swt/feat/*'`: here `*` crosses `/`, so the result also contains the children of `feat/foo`.
- `git for-each-ref refs/heads/swt/feat` (no `*`): a literal prefix, with the same error.

This command shows child **branches**. `swt list` shows child **worktrees**.

## TDD Fix Plan

Each cycle runs the real binary against a fixture repository, as the current end-to-end tests of `swt create` do. Every spawn of git sheds the inherited `GIT_*` environment through `gitscratch`.

1. **RED:** Write a test for a parent on branch `issue-42` and a parent on branch `feat/foo`. In each, `swt create fix-parser` prints one path. The directory is `<parent-worktree-name>--fix-parser-<token>.swt`, beside the parent. Its branch is `swt/<parent-branch>/fix-parser-<token>`, with the same token.
   **GREEN:** Give the naming step two more inputs: the parent branch and the parent worktree name. `swt create` reads the parent branch before it creates anything.
   *Existing expectations:* the tests that pin `swt/<name>-<token>` and `<name>-<token>.swt` change to the new format in this red commit, on purpose. The properties that they pin do not change: one token in both names, two concurrent creates of one name get two worktrees, the cleanup report names both, and `swt merge` accepts the printed path.

2. **RED:** Write a test for a parent on a detached HEAD. `swt create` exits 1, and stderr says that a detached HEAD has no branch to relate the child to. Stdout is empty. No worktree and no branch remain.
   **GREEN:** Refuse before `git worktree add` when HEAD is not a symbolic ref.

3. **RED:** Write a test for a parent with two children. `swt list` shows those two, one line each, path then branch, and exits 0. The bare `swt` usage names all three commands.
   **GREEN:** Add the `list` command. Read the worktree registry of git, and keep each entry whose branch starts with `swt/<current-branch>/`. This prefix rule is too loose on purpose. Cycle 4 makes it exact.

4. **RED:** Write a test with parents `feat` and `feat/foo`, each with one child. `swt list` in `feat` shows only the child of `feat`.
   **GREEN:** Parse the parent out of the branch (the text between `swt/` and the last `/`), and compare it for equality.

5. **RED:** Write a test for a parent with no children. Stdout is empty, stderr has a note, and the exit status is 0.
   **GREEN:** Write the note when the result is empty.

6. **RED:** Write a test for a child whose directory was deleted by hand. `swt list` still shows it, with the third field `prunable`.
   **GREEN:** Read the `prunable` line of the porcelain entry.

7. **RED:** Write a test for `swt list` on a detached HEAD. It exits 1 with a message on stderr.
   **GREEN:** Refuse when HEAD is not a symbolic ref. Share the check with cycle 2.

**REFACTOR:**

- Update the module docs of the command line and of the naming step. The commands no longer "each take exactly one argument".
- Add a test that runs the plain-git command from the design against parents `feat` and `feat/foo`, and compares the result with the branches that `swt list` shows. This test keeps the documented command true.
- Update the `swt` entry in `README.md` and its row in `TLDR.md`.
- Update `~/.claude/SWT.md` in the dotfiles repository, as a separate change there.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `swt create <name>` on branch `B` makes the branch `swt/B/<name>-<token>`, for `B` with and without `/`.
- [ ] The directory is `<parent-worktree-name>--<name>-<token>.swt`, beside the parent, with the same token as the branch.
- [ ] `swt create` on a detached HEAD refuses before it creates anything, and says why.
- [ ] `swt list` shows exactly the children of the current branch. It does not show the children of a branch that has the current branch as a prefix.
- [ ] A child with a missing directory shows with the field `prunable`.
- [ ] With no children, stdout is empty, stderr has a note, and the exit status is 0.
- [ ] `swt list` on a detached HEAD exits 1 with a message.
- [ ] The README, the TLDR, and the dotfiles `SWT.md` describe the new names, `swt list`, and the plain-git command.
- [ ] All new tests pass.
- [ ] Existing tests still pass. The only changed expectations are the name formats in cycle 1.

## Out of scope

- **`swt merge` from the wrong worktree.** `swt merge` merges into the worktree where it runs, whatever the parent of the child is. With the parent in the branch, it can refuse a child of a different branch. That changes the merge gate, and it gets its own issue.
- **Worktrees made before this change.** Their branches carry no parent, so `swt list` does not show them.
- **Child branches with no worktree**, for example after a teardown that failed. `swt list` shows worktrees. The plain-git command above shows branches.

## 6. Design Decisions

### D1 — Six fixed requests and explicit queue mode

Add only `queue` to the existing mode enum. The strict runtime JSON keeps its current fields: schema_version, mode, project_id, project_number, region, service_name, origin, database, namespace, users. Each of the exactly two users has email, subject, role, enabled. Queue mode requires both distinct subject bindings and all data-mode configuration. Old modes retain their current behavior and expose no catalog/list route. `GET /api/me` keeps the same keys; `request_id` is null in queue mode because no single request is selected globally. Its actor is always the verified caller.

The catalog is package-owned and fixed at six sources; users cannot select a file, namespace, source digest, catalog, or extra request through HTTP/config. Validate all sources and uniqueness before seeding. Fail with `FIXTURE_INVALID` on bad inventory. A new read-only map of stores is constructed by the launcher, using one existing Firestore client and the selected config. `create_app(..., *, catalog_stores=None)` requires exactly the catalog's six sources for queue mode, with keys matching sources, matching runtime config/database/namespace, and the original positional store identical to its catalog entry. Reject missing/mismatched dependencies as `CONFIG_INVALID` before storage writes; reject a catalog dependency in old modes. The map is copied before routes close over it.

### D2 — Preserve each request's storage contract

Keep schema version 1, the original source bytes/projection, payload hash function and original path. Paths remain `workflow_proofs/{namespace}/requests/{request_id}` with child `events/{operation_id}`. No legacy migration or reset is necessary. Seed each missing admitted request with the existing create-if-absent transaction; never write a decision during seeding. A partially completed startup is safe to retry because existing matching documents are validated and retained. Source mismatch stops startup; it is never repaired by overwriting documents. New IDs coexist with the original, and returning to handoff mode simply serves the original again without deleting the five additions.

Identifiers and wire shapes:

| Entity | Fields / contract |
|---|---|
| Request ID | 64 lowercase hex characters: SHA-256 of UTF-8 review_key, computed from the fixed packaged source. Membership in the catalog is also required. |
| Namespace | `proof_` plus lowercase hyphenated UUIDv4, chosen once privately; HTTP clients never supply it. |
| Operation ID | Lowercase hyphenated UUIDv4 from browser `crypto.randomUUID()`. Scoped to one request's events; the same ID on another request is a different operation, not a replay. |
| Source | schema_version=1, request_id, review_key, source_sha256, display. Display: ref, title, submitted_on ISO date, total two-decimal string, items[] with item_key, description, amount, category. |
| Request | Source fields plus state, next_owner_role, version (integer 0–100), created_at, updated_at. |
| Event | operation_id, payload_sha256, actor_sub, actor_label, actor_role, request_id, source_sha256, action, body, expected_version, previous_state, result_state, result_version, next_owner_role, created_at. |
| Actor | subject, email, label, role; verified per request, never accepted from request bodies. Public actor at `/api/me` is only the caller. |
| Timestamp | UTC RFC3339 string with six fractional digits and `Z`, serialized by existing `wire()`. |
| Mutation | Exactly operation_id, expected_version, body; decision adds exactly decision=`approve` or `not_approve`. Existing 8 KiB body/2,000-character comment limits apply. |

Every request retains its independent 100-event cap, version, full-history validation, same-operation retry and role checks. Queue mode permits the existing handoff actions; it introduces no new transition. Approval moves AWAITING_REVIEW → APPROVED with processor ownership; not-approval moves AWAITING_REVIEW → NOT_APPROVED with null owner; processor completion moves APPROVED → COMPLETED with null owner. Both terminal states permit comments without changing state/owner. Administrative completion never records a payment.

### D3 — A bounded summary over verified shared history

`GET /api/requests` returns exactly `{requests: RequestSummary[], request_count: 6, request_cap: 6}` in queue mode. RequestSummary has exactly request_id, display (ref/title/submitted_on/total only), state, next_owner_role, version, updated_at, latest_event. latest_event is null at version zero; otherwise it has exactly action, actor_label, actor_role, created_at from the last validated event. Do not return email, subject, raw comment body, source digest or full history in the list.

Build each summary from that store's existing validated `read(Deadline)` result. This deliberately reuses history integrity checking for six bounded requests, instead of introducing a second summary document or cross-request collection query. Execute the finite read loop outside the asynchronous web event loop through `run_in_threadpool`, sharing the incoming 20-second deadline; each database remote procedure call has an existing five-second maximum and mutation retries remain bounded. Stop and return the existing safe error envelope on any failure; no misleading partial-success count. Each row is consistent with its own returned version. The list is not an atomic snapshot across all requests; refresh resolves activity that happens while it is read. At most six histories of at most 100 events are read; output contains six summaries, never those histories.

Server ordering is updated_at descending, then request_id ascending for ties. Use timestamp values before serialization, not locale text. Browser filters preserve this order. Show latest event label/time, or “Awaiting first activity” for a new request. Counts derive from all six returned states; the visible row count separately reports matches after filters. Counts describe workflow, never paid/unpaid money.

### D4 — Routes and authorization

Both enabled pinned roles can see all six fictional requests. The server authenticates before catalog membership or storage access for list, HTML, static assets, detail and mutation routes. Membership lookup prevents access to any other document even if it exists in the same database. This is a two-person shared catalog, not request-specific user assignment.

| Method / route | Queue-mode behavior | Old-mode behavior |
|---|---|---|
| GET `/healthz` | Existing `{status:"ok"}`; no data | Unchanged |
| GET `/` | Queue HTML, role label, no embedded private roster | Existing identity/single-detail page |
| GET `/requests/{request_id}` | Selected request detail HTML and “All requests” link; unknown ID 404 | 404 |
| GET `/static/{name}` | Allowlisted queue and existing detail assets only | Existing assets; queue-only names 404 |
| GET `/api/me` | Existing actor shape, mode=`queue`, request_id=null | Existing mode-specific contract |
| GET `/api/requests` | D3 list response | 404 |
| GET `/api/requests/{request_id}` | `{request: Request, events: Event[], event_cap:100}` for an admitted source | Existing one-ID contract |
| POST `/api/requests/{request_id}/comments` | Both roles; `{receipt: Event}` | Existing comments/handoff behavior |
| POST `/api/requests/{request_id}/decision` | Reviewer only; `{receipt: Event}` | Existing handoff-only behavior |
| POST `/api/requests/{request_id}/complete` | Processor only; `{receipt: Event}` | Existing handoff-only behavior |

No query parameters on any protected route, including the list; use local filters. Unknown/malformed IDs are 404 after authentication. Invalid body/query is 400 INVALID_INPUT; unauthenticated is 401; wrong/disabled role or identity is 403. Keep conflict codes STALE_VERSION, OPERATION_CONFLICT, INVALID_TRANSITION, EVENT_CAP_REACHED and RETRY_CONFLICT; storage failure remains 503, source mismatch retains its existing startup error. Error shape remains `{error:{code,message,correlation_id}}`. Keep no-store, CSP (Content Security Policy), no-referrer, exact Origin/JSON/CSRF header rules, no CORS (cross-origin permission), safe logging, and text escaping. There is no role-switch UI or authentication fallback in production.

### D5 — Refresh and navigation that users can understand

Adopt the accepted preview's hierarchy and colors with semantic links, labeled search/select controls, keyboard focus indication, mobile scrolling and live feedback. Package CSS/JS separately to honor the existing CSP; do not serve the preview's inline script. A row opens the actual `/requests/{request_id}` page, not a modal with canned history. The selected page's data-request-id supplies every mutation path. Its existing forms keep operation IDs/drafts during ambiguous responses and never redirect a pending save to another request.

Fetch on initial queue entry, explicit Reload and browser `pageshow` restoration. Do not depend on browser back-cache returning fresh data. Disable Reload while pending; use a load sequence guard so an older response cannot replace a later one. Keep the old valid list visibly marked “Refresh failed; showing previously loaded requests” on a failed refresh; show no fake empty list/counts on initial failure. Session HTML/non-JSON or 401 prompts sign-in refresh. On success show when the queue was loaded. An empty filter result says “No requests match these filters” and offers a filter reset.

Keep filter state in the current page only for this first version: returning to `/` shows all requests and loads current data. This avoids introducing local storage or query-string exceptions. Status cards select that status; owner choices are Anyone, Reviewer, Processor, No further action (null). Search uses case-insensitive title/ref substring matching with trimmed input. It never searches comment bodies or private identity fields.

### D6 — Verify compatibility before cloud admission

Keep the Step 34 regression suite. Add real-component tests that capture the original source/request/events/receipts, enable queue mode in the same namespace, then assert the original projection and receipt replay are identical. Mutate two different requests and prove their versions/histories remain independent. Exercise two opposing same-request decisions with bounded conflict resolution; equal operation IDs across two different requests remain separate. Disabled users cannot list, navigate, mutate or replay; valid unknown IDs expose nothing. An inconsistent request makes the list fail safely. Test list ordering/counts/wire fields, zero/latest-event cases, failures, and one request reaching its cap without blocking another.

Use the existing local signer + loopback emulator + installed-wheel browser factory for repeatable UI evidence. ## Summary

The generated loopback MCP config for CLI backends unconditionally sets `alwaysLoad: true`, so every OpenClaw tool schema is eagerly expanded into the harness prompt on every turn and `tools.toolSearch` is silently a no-op on `claude-cli` runs. Derive that flag from resolved config instead of hardcoding it.

## Problem to solve

On CLI-backend runtimes OpenClaw does not build the model request; it exposes gateway tools to the child agent through the loopback MCP bridge (`bundleMcp`). The generated server entry is built in one place and always carries `alwaysLoad: true`:

```js
function createMcpServerConfig(port, headers) {
  return {
    mcpServers: {
      openclaw: {
        type: "http",
        url: `http://127.0.0.1:${port}/mcp`,
        alwaysLoad: true,
        headers,
      },
    },
  };
}
```

Both `createMcpLoopbackServerConfig()` and `createMcpAttachGrantServerConfig()` funnel through it, and there is no config input, plugin hook, or per-backend override.

Per the bundled Claude Agent SDK types, that flag means:

> When true, all tools from this server are always included in the prompt and never deferred behind tool search. Equivalent to setting `defer_loading: false` on the API. Default: tools are deferred when tool search is enabled. As a side effect this also blocks startup until the server is connected (capped at the standard 5s connect timeout) even though MCP startup is otherwise non-blocking by default.

So OpenClaw explicitly opts out of a deferral mechanism the harness already implements. This is observable: in the same Claude Code turn, other MCP servers are correctly deferred and their schemas are pulled on demand via `ToolSearch`, while all ~40 `mcp__openclaw__*` schemas are expanded up front.

`docs/tools/tool-search.md` documents `tools.toolSearch` as the answer to exactly this problem, but it is implemented only in the OpenClaw embedded runner. Operators whose primary model resolves to `agentRuntime.id: "claude-cli"` therefore have no knob at all — neither the OpenClaw-side one (does not apply to harness runs) nor the harness-side one (overridden by `alwaysLoad`).

### Measurements

Installed `openclaw@2026.9.1`, Claude Code `2.1.261`, `claude-cli` runtime, `tools.profile: "full"`, Telegram-only single agent:

| Prompt component                                                             | Approx. tokens |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------- |
| `mcp__openclaw__*` schemas (~40 tools)                                       | 13,000–14,000  |
| of which `message`                                                           | ~2,500         |
| of which `browser`                                                           | ~1,600         |
| of which `skill_workshop`                                                    | ~1,300         |
| Total static prefix (all schemas + system prompt + skills + workspace files) | ~36,000        |

The OpenClaw catalog is the single largest component of the static prefix, and the harness is already capable of deferring it.

## Proposed solution

Set `alwaysLoad` from resolved config rather than hardcoding it:

- When `tools.toolSearch` is enabled, omit `alwaysLoad` (or set it to `false`) in the generated MCP server entry, letting the harness defer OpenClaw tool schemas behind its own tool search.
- When `tools.toolSearch` is disabled, keep `alwaysLoad: true` so current behavior is unchanged by default.
- Optionally expose an explicit override for operators who want to decouple the two (`tools.toolSearch.cliBackendAlwaysLoad`, or a `bundleMcp` field on the backend registration).

The value of routing it through the existing key is portability: one operator-facing setting then means the same thing on the embedded runner (`code` / `tools` / `directory` modes) and on harness runtimes (native MCP deferral), so a config does not have to change when the selected model changes runtime.

Restricted runs that already pin an exact allowlist — for example the Claude node MCP listener that publishes only `mcp__openclaw__skill_workshop` — can keep eager loading; the flag matters for full catalogs.

## Alternatives considered

- **Patch the installed `dist` locally.** Works, but is lost on every upgrade and is not a solution for other operators.
- **Trim the catalog with `tools.deny`.** Removes capability. The point of tool search is to keep every tool reachable while paying for only the ones used.
- **Drop `agentRuntime.id` and run the same model over the provider API**, so the embedded runner applies `tools.toolSearch`. This changes billing from subscription to per-token, gives up the harness, and makes the config runtime-specific — the opposite of the goal.
- **Register a custom CLI backend plugin.** `api.registerCliBackend(...)` exposes `bundleMcp` / `bundleMcpMode`, but the MCP server entry itself is generated in core, so a plugin cannot shape this field.

## Impact

- **Affected:** every operator on `claude-cli` — the documented default path for Claude Code and subscription users — and any future `bundleMcp` backend whose harness supports deferred MCP tools.
- **Severity:** performance and cost. Nothing is functionally broken; the run is just larger than it needs to be.
- **Frequency:** always. Every turn of every session, plus every scheduled heartbeat and cron turn.
- **Consequence:** ~13–14k tokens per request that the harness is already able to defer. With the default 30-minute heartbeat that alone is ~48 extra turns/day carrying the full catalog on turns whose entire output is `NO_REPLY`. On a subscription route this surfaces directly as quota burn rather than a line item.

## Evidence / examples

- Generated config: `createMcpServerConfig()` in the MCP HTTP loopback runtime module (`dist/mcp-http.loopback-runtime-*.js` in the published package), used by `createMcpLoopbackServerConfig()` and `createMcpAttachGrantServerConfig()`.
- A second hardcoded occurrence for the Claude node MCP listener in the daemon bundle, which pins `--allowedTools mcp__openclaw__skill_workshop`.
- `alwaysLoad` semantics: `dist/extensions/anthropic/agent-sdk/sdk.d.ts` (`McpHttpServerConfig`, `McpSdkServerConfigWithInstance`).
- `docs/tools/tool-search.md` — "Tool Search is an experimental OpenClaw agent runtime feature"; describes no CLI-backend path.
- `docs/gateway/cli-backends.md` — "OpenClaw does not inject tool calls into the CLI backend protocol. Backends only see gateway tools when they opt into `bundleMcp: true`."
- Related: #14785 is the canonical tracker for tool-schema overhead on the embedded runner (message-tool schema shape, Tooling prompt section, cron description). This report is the CLI-backend-side gap, which that tracker does not cover: here the schemas are not OpenClaw's to shrink, only OpenClaw's to defer. #16076 requested Anthropic `defer_loading` support and was closed as stale.

## Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes — happy to implement it, pending maintainer sign-off on the config shape (reuse `tools.toolSearch` vs. a dedicated key).

## Additional information

Backward compatibility: with `tools.toolSearch` unset or `false`, the generated config is byte-identical to today's. The behavior change only reaches operators who have already opted into tool search, and it makes that opt-in mean the same thing on both runtime families.

# An Analytics surface — the owner's ask, and the one decision that splits it into two different Issues

**Owner ask, 2026-09-11, verbatim:**

> «as metricas do nosso GA poderiam virar uma sessao do site Analytics. assim demonstro minha competencia e consigo ler as metricas de uma forma mais agradavel para meu proprio entendimento. Agrego meu tom critico sobre como eu gosto de acompanhar analytics de plataformas digitais. Agrega a defesa do meu perfil profissional.»

`product` · `reader-facing`. **Intake run 2026-09-11 against `-io` `origin/main` = `3f7c7d6`**, both leads dispatched in isolation. **`ready` is NOT applied** — one decision is the owner's and the description cannot close without it.

<!-- owner-take: supplied -->
> «Agrego meu tom critico sobre como eu gosto de acompanhar analytics de plataformas digitais.»

---

## THE DECISION THIS ISSUE IS WAITING ON

**Does this page carry GA4's FIGURES, or what the repository knows about its OWN MEASUREMENT?**

Both leads reached this independently and neither will decide it. They are **different Issues with different preconditions**, and describing them as one is `/definition-of-ready`'s flagship failure arriving at filing time:

- **the numbers page** — GA4 counts. Needs a credential decision, a generator, a staleness answer, and a new record.
- **the schema page** — what is emitted, what each measurement can and cannot establish, what is deliberately not concluded. **Buildable today, no credential, no network.**

Everything below is downstream of that one answer.

---

## The ask is THREE artifacts under one name, and the split is clean

| his reason | what actually serves it | on this site? |
|---|---|---|
| **read the metrics pleasantly, for himself** | **`-skills#401`** — the funnel rite, `ready`, `sp:8`, already queued | **no.** A published page is a *worse* tool than the console he already has: the console is live, the page is a transcription with a staleness clock |
| **demonstrate competence** | a published argument, his numbers as the worked example | **yes** |
| **his critical tone + the professional case** | the same artifact | **yes** |

**Purpose 2 gets an explicit no.** A page that serves him must update often; a page that serves a reader must age well. Those are opposite requirements on one file, and every design satisfying both lands on a dashboard stale for him *and* rotting for the reader. It is not dropped — it is pointed at the Issue that already owns it.

---

## The measured argument that decides the shape: this site already ran this experiment and it is failing right now

`/architecture` publishes a hand-typed count of the decision library. **It is false in both editions, today:**

```
ls docs/adr/[0-9]*.md | wc -l                                                   # -> 51
node -e "console.log(require('./apps/fed/src/content/generated/adrs.json').length)"  # -> 51
grep -rnoE "[0-9]+ decis(ões|ions)" apps/fed/src/content/architecture.{pt,en}.md
# -> architecture.en.md:299: 49 decisions
#    architecture.pt.md:301: São 49 decisões
```

**False since 2026-09-04 — seven days — and it went false inside the very slice that shipped the analytics events this proposal wants to publish.**

**The page predicted its own failure.** Its prose says the `49` is typed by hand and that cutting the rendered table removed the binding that kept it honest. It predicted, shipped anyway, and the failure arrived in ten days.

**That is the empirical answer to *what would publishing these numbers argue*.** Not a hypothesis — a measured instance, on the same page, on the surface whose whole thesis is that the inventory is *derived*. A `/analytics` page of hand-transcribed GA4 figures is that defect with a faster clock and a bigger surface: GA4 moves daily, the ADR library moves weekly.

**This finding is tracked separately and is not this Issue's to fix** — see the closing note.

### And the owner has already published the criterion that excludes a GA4 figure

`apps/fed/src/content/architecture.pt.md:279` declines to publish a measured token figure and states why:

> *«O número não é publicado porque a fonte é uma transcrição de sessão privada, que gate nenhum alcança.»*

**GA4 is exactly that class** — a private console, no credential, no gate reaches it. So a page of GA4 figures does not merely risk staleness; **it contradicts a criterion already live on the site.** Any numbers version must say out loud that its source is a console no gate reaches, and that the figure is transcribed on a stated date.

---

## The two leads' positions — recorded as a disagreement, deliberately not resolved

### `product-lead` — BUILD, rescoped and sequenced

**Verified rather than inherited: the five zeros are a behaviour fact, not a wiring fact.** Every one of the eight events has an emitter *and* a mounted caller:

```
for f in trackArticleEndReached trackArticleProgress trackShareComplete trackContactClick \
         trackShareOpen trackContactReach trackOutboundClick trackNavClick; do
  grep -rl "$f" apps/fed/src --include='*.ts' --include='*.tsx' \
    | grep -v '\.test\.' | grep -v 'lib/analytics.ts'; done
# -> useArticleProgress · ShareLinks · ShareModal · useContactClicks
#    ShareButton · useContactReach · useOutboundClicks · AppShell
```

**That matters: the zeros are honestly zero and are publishable as zeros.** Dead wiring would have made them a false floor.

**Priced both ways, and this is the positioning call:**

- **Most honest thing on the site, if the numbers are evidence.** `/architecture` already publishes a small unflattering measured figure — R$ 34,31/month — with the arithmetic shown and an admission of waste found late. In that register a small number is an **asset**: the number is small and the method is rigorous, and the method is what is being sold.
- **A liability if the numbers are the headline**, and the asymmetry is not subtle: the cost figure is about a **system he controls**; the analytics figure is about an **audience he does not**. A reader forgives a small bill and reads discipline into it. The same reader reads a small audience as *nobody is listening* — on the surface whose job is to get him hired.

**The resulting design constraint, and it is a constraint rather than a preference:** *the numbers are admissible as evidence inside an argument and inadmissible as the page's headline.* **If the top of the fold is a figure, it is the wrong page.**

**The best material in the whole proposal is already measured:** `contact_reach` fires and `contact_click` never has. **The career funnel leaks at the LAST step, not the first.** An essay whose worked example is *"I instrumented my own hiring funnel and found nobody takes the last step"* is the competence demonstration and the honest-journey pillar in one paragraph, and it costs nothing to write.

**Thin first slice: an ARTICLE, not a route.** Three reasons, in weight order — a route has no distribution at this traffic level while the content lane ships a LinkedIn + X pair in the same batch; it tests the subject before buying the surface (ADR-0046's earn-its-place pattern); and it is cheap to be wrong, where a route is a permanent URL contract plus an OG card and nav label per locale plus a new `NavArea` member on a schema ADR-0051 declares immutable once shipped.

**How we would know it worked:** primarily, **does `contact_click` fire at all** — it never has, and it is the platform's stated purpose. Secondarily, `share_complete` against the article baseline. **The honest caveat: at this traffic none of these is evaluable for months, and a null result at n≈35 is not evidence of failure.** That constraint is itself an argument for the article shape — an article can be judged on whether it was worth writing.

### `tech-lead` — ADJUST; the direction is right, the data source is not

**Buildable under ADR-0002/0004: yes, and not marginally.** ADR-0043's shape holds without amendment — a generator writes a committed manifest, the build reads only the manifest, CI compares. A GA4-sourced `analytics.json` would be a fourth file beside `adrs.json`, `diagrams.json`, `harness.json`, and would break no invariant.

**The obstacle is one layer in, and it is precise: ADR-0043's chosen option is a second checkout of a PUBLIC repo with NO credential, and its rejected option 3 is reading the source at generation time over the network.** What is proposed is 0043's shape with 0043's rejected source. **The warrant does not transfer.**

**And this repository has already ruled on a network-sourced generator, in a file nobody cited.** `apps/fed/scripts/check-video-embeddable.mjs` is the only script in the tree that makes a third-party call (`grep -n "fetch(" apps/fed/scripts/*.mjs` → **one** match). Its header:

> *"A build that reddens because YouTube is unreachable converts someone else's outage into our own red pipeline, and the first response to a red that nobody caused is to relax it — which is how a gate becomes theatre. So this script is wired into NO workflow, NO test run and NO build step."*
>
> *"It also does not WRITE. **A script that edited `videos.json` from a third party's answer would put an unreviewed claim into the repository on a schedule.**"*

**The second half transfers exactly** — that is what a stats page is.

#### The credential question, answered rather than deferred — and the orchestrator's brief was WRONG about it

**The 2026-09-10 ruling does NOT foreclose a CI service account, and this Issue records that correction because the intake brief asserted the opposite.** `-skills#401`'s own route table marks the credential route *not chosen*, and says its rejection *"was argued about unattended writes; no credential is held on the chosen route, so the argument is not engaged at all."* He chose a route for **an agent rite**, between an unfireable attended paste and a credential **an agent holds mid-dispatch**. **A GitHub Actions job is neither** — no `agent_type`, no dispatch, no hook layer to be ungated by.

**What it would cost — measured, every secret these workflows reference:**

```
grep -rhoE "secrets\.[A-Z_]+" .github/workflows/*.yml | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
#  3 VERSION_BUMP_TOKEN · 2 TFC_API_TOKEN · 2 BUDGET_ALERT_EMAIL
#  2 AWS_INFRA_OIDC_ROLE_ARN · 1 SONAR_TOKEN · 1 CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN · 1 AWS_FED_OIDC_ROLE_ARN
```

Seven — every one an AWS role **ARN**, a token for a tool already in the loop, or an email. **A GA4 service-account JSON key would be the first long-lived static private credential in this repository**, and ADR-0015's rejected option 2 is *"long-lived AWS access keys as secrets — leakable, rotation burden, over-scoped."* **A static Google key is that rejected option wearing another provider's badge: RECONSIDER.**

**A third route neither the ask nor `#401` enumerated: Google Workload Identity Federation** — federating the GitHub OIDC token this repo already mints into a Google service account **with no stored key**, the structural twin of `AWS_*_OIDC_ROLE_ARN`. **Flagged as a hypothesis, not a measurement.** Nothing in the tree touches it (`grep -rn "analyticsdata|googleapis|google-analytics-data|runReport"` → no output; calibrated against `gtag|GA_MEASUREMENT` → **28 files**, so the zero is real). Whether GA4's Data API accepts a federated principal is the one thing to confirm before anyone budgets it.

**And `-io#639` is evidence about instinct, not a ruling on a new credential class** — he refused *widening the read scope of an existing* secret. Report it at that strength.

#### The operational half — this is where the design fails, BEFORE the credential question is reached

**Trigger — there is no good one.** On merge puts a third-party call in the deploy path, which is `check-video-embeddable`'s named refusal. Scheduled is ADR-0043's rejected shape, and even where its objection weakens (a PR has an author by construction) it is a cron writing numbers nobody asked for into a public repo. Manual means the page is as fresh as the last time he remembered.

**Failure must not redden the build.** Non-negotiable and already argued in this tree.

**Staleness is the one with no answer, and the precedent has a measured cost.** `/architecture` already confesses the equivalent: *"The eighth persona landed in the plugin on 2026-08-31; this job was still being skipped on 2026-09-03, and it first ran on 2026-09-06 — red, on an unrelated pull request… **Six days, and sixty-seven runs of this workflow went by without that comparison running once.**"*

**And the high merge cadence buys nothing** — 135 merges in 30 days is how often the *site* redeploys, not how often the *manifest* regenerates.

**The decisive asymmetry: for `harness.json`, stale means a check eventually goes red. For an analytics manifest the number is never *wrong* in a way anything can detect** — it was true on its generation date, and no check in either repository can compare it to a property this build cannot read. **A drift check is unavailable in principle**; only a date stamp, which ADR-0043 rejected by name: *"a stamp makes staleness legible and does nothing to make it detectable."*

**So the manifest pattern's shape comes along and its guarantee does not** — on the one page whose thesis is that every claim resolves to something a reader can open.

#### The no-credential alternative is a DIFFERENT and BETTER thing, not a lesser one

**The critical tone the ask wants is already written, in `analytics.ts`, at a depth no dashboard reaches:**

> *`share_complete`, **which CANNOT SEE A COMPLETED SHARE**. Both entry points open the destination in a new tab, so what the page observes is that a composer was opened — never that anything was posted.*
>
> *`article_end_reached`, NOT `read`. **Nothing a browser can see proves a read.***

**A page built from that is a page about what a measurement can and cannot establish** — a senior-engineering claim. A page of GA4 counts is a page of counts, which any tool prints.

**And it is the only version whose numbers survive the site's own honesty constraints.** ADR-0033 is a hard opt-in gate; ADR-0023 already records that usage numbers are *a floor, not exact*. **So every GA4 figure is a floor of a floor — consented readers minus blockers — and the site cannot know its own denominator, by construction.**

**Its ceiling, stated so it is not oversold:** it shows what is measured and what each measurement can bear. It shows **no outcomes**. It does not serve purpose 2 at all.

**One gap it cannot close:** ADR-0051's registration step is outside every gate and nothing in the app tree names it (`grep -rlni "custom dimension"` → the two ADR files and nothing else). A page asserting *"this parameter is queryable"* asserts something **no artifact here knows**. It can honestly say *what is emitted*; it cannot say *what is queryable*. **That distinction belongs on the page, not in a comment.**

### Where they differ, and it is one axis

`product-lead` argues value: competence, the professional case, an unusual and credible surface. **`tech-lead` does not dispute any of it** — and answers on the same axis from the other side:

> **This would be the first number on the site the reader cannot falsify and the build cannot check.** Every other figure on `/architecture` resolves to a file, a manifest and a comparison. A GA4 figure resolves to a property nobody but the owner can open. On the one page whose argument is *whoever makes the claim produces the evidence*, publishing an unfalsifiable number is a bigger positioning cost than the feature is a positioning gain.

**`product-lead` stated in advance what would move it:** *"if `tech-lead` can produce a generator that reaches GA4 without a credential in the build, that dissolves my strongest objection and I would withdraw the RESCOPE down to a plain BUILD."* **It could not.** The one thing it would not concede on any mechanism: **the numbers are evidence inside an argument, never the page's headline.**

---

## The coupling nobody had named, and it must be decided at intake rather than discovered in the build

**`NavArea` is a closed union serving two registered GA4 custom dimensions** (`nav_click`'s `from` and `to`), with **10** members at head. Giving `/analytics` a nav entry adds an 11th — to a vocabulary **ADR-0051 makes immutable once shipped and non-retroactive**.

> **The page that reports the funnel would modify the funnel's own schema, and its own dimension value would have zero history on the day it ships.**

**And skipping the member is worse: the page collapses into `other` silently — measured, no test fails.**

## What a ROUTE drags in

**Charting is a new tool-class.** `apps/fed` runs 13 runtime dependencies. **ADR-0047 already set the bar** for a figure Mermaid cannot draw — authored SVG, fixed geometry, real text labels, arrangement asserted arithmetically — and its drivers are non-negotiable: *the reader with JS off must get the figure*, *labels must be real text*, *a wrong picture must fail before it is served*. **Most charting libraries render client-side and fail the first driver outright.**

**Two locales, not optional:** 2 prerendered routes, 2 OG cards, 2 sitemap entries, 2 content editions. **Number and date formatting is a real cost on a page made of figures** — `pt-BR` and `en` disagree on decimal separator, thousands separator and date order, and there is no locale-formatting layer in `src/lib/` today.

**Obligatory mechanical surfaces:** `scripts/routes.mjs` (`STATIC_ROUTES`), `src/App.tsx`, `src/components/AppShell.tsx` (`NAV`), `src/i18n/messages.ts`, `src/lib/navArea.ts`, `scripts/og-copy.mjs`, and the `e2e/routes.spec.ts` / `seo.spec.ts` / `per-locale.spec.ts` suites. Sitemap and prerender follow from `routes.mjs` automatically — named so nobody pays for it twice.

## What is owed on the record

- **ADR-0004 — not amended.** The committed-manifest pattern already satisfies it.
- **ADR-0023 — amended, pointing out.** It scoped observability to what a static site can *produce*; publishing that telemetry is a new thing it never considered.
- **A NEW record is owed**, its subject being whichever version lands. It crosses the significance bar on new tool-class, cross-cutting pattern, and — credentialed — a public credential surface. **`tech-lead` writes it, in the implementing MR.**
- **ADR-0043 gets an amendment only if its pattern is genuinely reused with a network source**, because that is its rejected option 3.

## Ordering

**The product lane is nearly empty** — `{"open":47,"ready":14}`, of which **one** is `product`-typed and thirteen are `content`. So opportunity cost is near zero and this can be taken soon.

**But it must not go first, and the reason is supply chain rather than priority:** `-skills#401` is what gets the data out from behind the login. **Building the page before the rite gives it nothing to publish except a hand-transcription — the `49 decisões` failure reproduced deliberately.** Sequence: `-skills#401` → the article → the route, if earned.

## Class

**boundary** — it is reader-facing, it publishes claims on the surface that argues the platform's rigor, and the credentialed variant opens a new credential surface. *Significance beats in-pattern.*

## Not applied, and why

**`ready` is withheld.** The description cannot close until the owner answers the one decision at the top. Both leads said so independently; `tech-lead` added that describing both versions as one Issue is `/definition-of-ready`'s flagship failure at filing time.
